name: Mukhanov-Brandenberger Universe with Limiting Curvature
description: Homogeneous and isotropic universes in a theory of gravity changed at Planck curvatures so that no curvature invariant can grow without limit. A closed universe that collapses becomes de Sitter space, bounces, and expands again, and without matter every solution oscillates about flat spacetime or approaches de Sitter space. Viatcheslav Mukhanov and Robert Brandenberger proposed the theory in 1992 and worked out its universes with Andrew Sornborger in 1993.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history:
The speed of light bounds every velocity, and Planck's constant bounds the smallest cell of phase space in which a particle can be found [brandenberger1993]. Newton's constant sets no such limit in Einstein's theory, where a collapsing universe reaches infinite curvature in a finite time [brandenberger1993, brandenberger1995]. Moissei Markov postulated in 1982 a limiting density for all forms of matter, at which the differences between its kinds disappear, and in a homogeneous and isotropic universe that density brings on a phase of de Sitter space [brandenberger1995]. A few years later the limit moved to the curvature itself: for every solution of the gravitational equations, a black hole's included, the curvature stays below a greatest value, expected at the Planck scale [brandenberger1995]. The limit puts a piece of de Sitter space inside a black hole where the singularity would be, the picture of Valeri Frolov, Markov, and Viatcheslav Mukhanov from 1989 [brandenberger1993, frolov1989].¶Viatcheslav Mukhanov and Robert Brandenberger built a theory whose homogeneous and isotropic universes obey that limit in 1992, and with Andrew T. Sornborger they worked out its universes in 1993 [mukhanov1992nonsingular, brandenberger1993]. Their guide was a free particle: add to its Newtonian Lagrangian $m\dot x^2/2$ the term $m\left(\phi\dot x^2 - V(\phi)ight)$, with $\phi$ a field that has no dynamics of its own, and the equation for $\phi$ sets $\dot x^2 = V'(\phi)$ [brandenberger1993]. A potential whose slope is bounded bounds the velocity, and with $V = 2\phi^2/(1 + 2\phi)$, in units with $c = 1$, the action with $\phi$ eliminated is that of a particle in special relativity, up to a constant that changes no equation of motion [brandenberger1993]. The device of such a field, a Lagrange multiplier, is Boris Altshuler's [brandenberger1993].¶In gravity two such fields multiply two curvature invariants, and the first is $$I_1 = R - \sqrt{3}\left(4R_{\mu
u}R^{\mu
u} - R^2ight)^{1/2},$$ which is $12H^2$ in a spatially flat homogeneous and isotropic universe with Hubble rate $H$, the square root taken with the sign of $\dot H$ [brandenberger1993]. The second is $I_2 = 4R_{\mu
u}R^{\mu
u} - R^2$, entering as $-\sqrt{I_2}$, which among spatially flat homogeneous and isotropic universes vanishes for de Sitter space alone, flat spacetime counted as de Sitter space with $H = 0$ [brandenberger1993]. The potential of the first field bounds $I_1$, and the potential of the second tends to a constant as its field grows, which drives $I_2$ to zero [brandenberger1993].¶For a universe with scale factor $a(t)$ and spatial curvature $k$, in units with $c = 1$, the two constraints are $$H^2 +  rac{k}{a^2} =  rac{V_1'(\phi_1)}{12},\qquad \dot H -  rac{k}{a^2} = - rac{V_2'(\phi_2)}{\sqrt{12}}$$ [brandenberger1993]. With the potentials they chose, $V_1'$ rises toward $12H_0^2$ and never reaches it, so $H^2 + k/a^2$ stays below $H_0^2$, with $H_0$ a constant they expected at the Planck scale [brandenberger1993]. A closed universe, $k = 1$, can then never be smaller than $1/H_0$. For a black hole the invariant $I_2$ is not enough, since it vanishes on the Schwarzschild metric too, and a term in the square of the Weyl tensor has to be added [brandenberger1993].¶Without matter, the flat universes of the theory either oscillate about Minkowski space or approach de Sitter space, and each one continues to $t = \pm\infty$ [brandenberger1993]. A contracting flat universe outside the periodic class approaches contracting de Sitter space and takes an infinite time to do so [brandenberger1993]. A closed universe that would end in a big crunch under Einstein's equations heads toward de Sitter space in the same way, until the curvature of its space takes over [brandenberger1993]. Within a time of about $1/H_0$ its Hubble rate changes sign, a de Sitter bounce, and it expands again [brandenberger1993]. The Weyl tensor of de Sitter space vanishes, so the theory meets Roger Penrose's hypothesis that the Weyl tensor vanishes at the beginning and end of the universe [brandenberger1993].¶Dust and radiation retain their usual equations of motion, and the gravitational equations contain the added curvature terms [brandenberger1993]. Matter loses its hold near the limit: the coupling of matter to geometry goes to zero as spacetime approaches de Sitter space, which they called asymptotic freedom [brandenberger1993]. With matter added, the universes near Minkowski space approach de Sitter space as well [brandenberger1993]. An expanding universe of the theory begins in de Sitter space, with $a \propto e^{Ht}$ for $k = 0$, or comes out of a de Sitter bounce for $k = 1$, so it has a period of inflation driven by gravity [brandenberger1993].¶Brandenberger and coauthors added a dilaton in 1998 and found spatially flat universes that bounce with a different multiplier potential [brandenberger1998]. Their curvature stays finite along each solution, and the greatest curvature depends on the solution [brandenberger1998]. Damien A. Easson and Brandenberger extended the construction to the string frame in 1999; the dilaton can diverge, and they assumed a potential to stabilize it [easson1999]. Philipp Höffer v. Loewenfeld and Ivo Sachs investigated anisotropic contraction in 2008 and found evidence for a continuation through a nearly flat phase, with finite Riemann components and divergent curvature derivatives [loewenfeld2008]. Abhik Kumar Sanyal quantized the constrained homogeneous isotropic theory in 2009 and obtained a Wheeler-DeWitt equation with a semiclassical time parameter [sanyal2009].¶Daisuke Yoshida, Jerome Quintin, Masahide Yamaguchi, and Brandenberger found in 2017 that the cosmological perturbations of the model carry Ostrogradski instabilities unless the action contains the square of the Weyl tensor with the right coefficient [yoshida2017]. In two nonsingular scenarios built on it, one of them inflationary, they found ghost and gradient instabilities through most of the cosmic evolution [yoshida2017]. Yoshida and coauthors also introduced invariants from covariant derivatives of the Ricci scalar and found genesis trajectories free of ghost and gradient instabilities; their genesis example could not recover a universe containing matter at late times [yoshida2017]. Ali Chamseddine and Mukhanov returned to limiting curvature in 2017 with a modification of the longitudinal mode of gravity, in which contracting Friedmann and Kasner universes bounce in a time inversely proportional to the square root of the limiting curvature [chamseddine2017].¶Yoshida and Brandenberger studied spherical geometries in 2018 and found singular solutions even when all quadratic curvature invariants remained finite [yoshida2018spherical]. The extra fields diverged or their radial evolution equations became singular at a finite radius [yoshida2018spherical]. Yoshida and Quintin showed in 2018 that the asymptotic de Sitter boundary of inflationary universes built from derivatives of the Ricci scalar is smoothly extendible, with $\dot H/a^2$ tending to zero [yoshida_quintin2018].¶Quintin and Yoshida bounded the trace of extrinsic curvature in cuscuton gravity in 2020 and found flat bounces whose linear perturbations remain finite when $H = 0$ [quintin2020]. Yuki Sakakihara and coauthors bounded both the Hubble rate and anisotropy in a Bianchi I universe in 2020; freedom from ghost instabilities depended on the directions of the perturbation wavevectors and the initial conditions [sakakihara2020]. The anisotropic universes have finite scalar curvature invariants; completeness of null geodesics remained open [sakakihara2020].¶Frolov and Andrei Zelnikov bounded the curvature with inequality constraints in 2021, and a closed universe of thermal radiation then bounces through a stage close to de Sitter space [frolov2021bouncing]. Frolov and Zelnikov applied two curvature inequalities to a spherical black hole interior in 2022; the axial direction expands exponentially and the radius of its spheres oscillates [frolov2022blackholes]. Andrei V. Frolov and Valeri Frolov examined changes between constrained and unconstrained motion in 2023 and found that the control field must vanish at a change of regime, with further matching conditions when the constraint contains higher derivatives [frolov2023].¶Amir Dehghani, Ghazal Geshnizjani, and Quintin carried the cuscuton bounce calculation to cubic order in scalar perturbations in 2025 [cuscuton2025]. For a massless matter field, Dehghani and coauthors found cuscuton parameters for which the strong coupling scale stays above the background energy scale and the bounce generates negligible non-Gaussianity on cosmological scales [cuscuton2025]. The amplitude of the observable curvature bispectrum also depends on the conversion of entropy perturbations into curvature perturbations [cuscuton2025].

related.text: The space every universe of the theory approaches as its curvature nears the limit, with a Hubble rate no greater than $H_0$ [brandenberger1993]. A closed universe turns around through a de Sitter bounce, which resembles the waist of de Sitter's closed universe [brandenberger1993].

Friedmann's metric with any scale factor. With the scale factor taken from field equations that keep $H^2 + k/a^2$ below $H_0^2$, it is this universe, and it reaches no big bang and no big crunch [brandenberger1993].

A flat universe of a massless scalar field whose contraction turns into expansion at a greatest density, about 0.41 of the Planck density, from the quantum geometry of loop quantum cosmology [ashtekar2009bianchi, ashtekar2011status]. There a flat universe bounces; with a limiting curvature a flat universe contracts toward de Sitter space for all time, and only a closed one bounces [brandenberger1993].

A black hole of Einstein's theory whose centre is de Sitter space, with every curvature invariant finite [ayonbeato2000]. Applied to a black hole, the limit on curvature puts de Sitter space where the singularity would be, as Valeri Frolov, Moissei Markov, and Viatcheslav Mukhanov proposed in 1989 [brandenberger1993, frolov1989].

A black hole whose core is de Sitter space of radius $\ell$ whatever its mass [hayward2006]. Valeri Frolov showed in 2016 that its curvature stays below a value of order $1/\ell^2$ for every mass, the condition Markov proposed and this theory builds into its field equations [frolov2016, brandenberger1993].

coordinates.name: Comoving

parameters.description: Scale factor ($a > 0$), a length, the radius of curvature of space at the time $t$, with the Hubble rate $H = (da/dt)/a$. The field equations of the theory hold $H^2 + c^2/a^2$ below $H_0^2$, so $a$ stays above $c/H_0$
The limiting Hubble rate of the theory, an inverse time, expected at the Planck scale

coordinates.convention: We use cosmic time $t$ and the angles $(\chi, \theta, \phi)$ of the unit 3-sphere about one observer, with $a\chi$ the distance from that observer. The scale factor $a(t)$ is the radius of curvature of space, a length, and we leave it free, since no solution is known in closed form. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, a prime is $a' = da/d(ct)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: de Sitter Bounce

parameters.description: Radius of the 3-sphere at the bounce $t = 0$, a length, with $\ell > c/H_0$ for the limiting Hubble rate $H_0$ of the theory. At the time $t$ the radius is $a = \ell\cosh(ct/\ell)$ and the Hubble rate $H = (c/\ell)\tanh(ct/\ell)$, so $H^2 + c^2/a^2 = c^2/\ell^2$ at every time
